overview.text: The Four Freedoms are a series of four paintings by American illustrator Norman Rockwell, inspired by President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s January 6, 1941 address describing freedoms he hoped would shape the postwar world: freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want, and freedom from fear. Rockwell made the ideas visible through familiar scenes of everyday life rather than abstract symbols. The Saturday Evening Post published the paintings in 1943, and they later became part of a nationwide war-bond campaign. Their combination of accessible domestic imagery and wartime ideals made the series a widely circulated visual expression of the purposes associated with the Allied war effort.

key_facts.text: Roosevelt outlined the four freedoms in a January 6, 1941 message to Congress.
The four titles are Freedom of Speech, Freedom of Worship, Freedom from Want, and Freedom from Fear.
Rockwell translated the broad ideals into scenes of ordinary American life.
The Saturday Evening Post published the paintings in 1943; each appeared with an accompanying essay.
Freedom from Want shows a festive meal shared by three generations, though the people posing as a family were not all biologically related.
